sweep_summary: Three target items for Mundari (mund1320; catalog classification conflict between Hoffmann 1903 initial, Cook 1965 closed-final-attracts, Sinha 1975, Osada 1992/2008, and the Horo/Anderson instrumental line). Two were obtained and read in full as open author copies recovered through Internet Archive copy of Donegan's University of Hawaii 'Papers' directory (the live ling.hawaii.edu paths now 404): Donegan 1993 (LTBA 16(1):1-43; also two SEAlang scans, one scanned) and Donegan & Stampe 2004 (YSALL 2004:3-36; publisher DOI 10.1515/9783110179897.3 closed). Both are family-level typological essays: Munda word accent is 'falling'/initial, with light+heavy disyllables accenting the heavy second syllable and longer words keeping the accent on the second syllable from the left; Sora is the exemplar and Mundari is never given an accent statement, so they refine the reading of the catalog conflict (Hoffmann and Cook become two faces of one weight-conditioned left-edge rule) without deciding Mundari's coding. Anderson 2020 (Brill, ch.6 pp.157-197, doi 10.1163/9789004425606_008) is paywalled (Brill bot-wall, Unpaywall closed, no PAR/Living Tongues copy); only its abstract was read via an Internet Archive copy, and it is silent on Mundari word stress; priority medium (Harvard e-access). An extra open item, Donegan & Stampe 2002 (BLS 28S:111-120), was downloaded and is silent on Mundari accent. No first-hand Mundari stress statement was found; the catalog's deciding sources are not superseded. all lookups were done by direct download (Crossref, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar API, the Internet Archive).

new_statements.quote: Although Munda accent is word-initial, in iambic words, i.e. words in which a light (open) initial syllable precedes a heavy (closed or long-voweled) second syllable, most Munda languages treat the light initial syllable as an anacrusis or pickup syllable, and put the heavy second syllable on the accent, as in Sora ebɔy 'one'. Disyllabic words of iambic shape thus have accent on the final syllable. In Munda such words are common enough that some observers, noting this final accent but not investigating what kind of rule puts it there, have concluded that Munda languages have final accent. But if additional syllables are added to such words in Munda, the accent stays on the second syllable from the beginning of the word.
new_statements.citation: Donegan, Patricia (1993). Rhythm and vocalic drift in Munda and Mon-Khmer. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 16(1): 1-43 (author copy via the Internet Archive of ling.hawaii.edu/faculty/donegan/Papers/).
new_statements.locator: p.5, section 2 'Opposite accentuations, opposite structures' (PDF page 5 of the author copy; same wording confirmed in the scanned of the SEAlang scan)
new_statements.reading: A family-level (Munda) rule, illustrated with Sora and not with Mundari data: word accent is initial, except that a light initial syllable before a heavy (closed/long) second syllable is treated as an anacrusis and the heavy second syllable is accented; in longer words the accent stays on the second syllable from the left rather than tracking the word end; balanced LL/HH words are initial-accented. Read against the catalog's conflict record it makes Hoffmann 1903 (generally initial) and Cook 1965 (final if closed, else penult, in disyllables) two faces of one left-edge, weight-conditioned rule, and it agrees with the carried Osada 2008/Sinha 1975 reports that trisyllables are never initial. It is impressionistic and not first-hand for Mundari, so it cannot decide the Mundari coding; the held Horo et al. 2023/2025 instrumental studies (no robust word-level prominence cue) remain the most direct Mundari evidence.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog codes Mundari as 'conflict' (qs-tier-2026-09-12, no rule) and the existing Donegan 1993 statement already carries Cook 1965 second-hand as 'final if closed, else penult, in disyllables'. This first-hand reading confirms that pole verbatim and adds three details the carried report lacks: (i) Cook restricts the rule to the MORPHEME and declines to state a word-stress rule; (ii) at word level he reports root-retention with unstressed suffixes, i.e. stress does not migrate rightward onto formatives, so his 'final/penult' is not a right-edge word rule; (iii) diphthongs attract stress. Against Donegan's family-level left-edge account (initial, but LH -> second) Cook agrees on CV.CV (i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Within the morpheme (mono-, di- and the rare trisyllabic morphemes built of CV and CVC syllables): stress the final syllable if it is closed (CVC); otherwise stress the penultimate. Cook states the rule only for the morpheme domain and says explicitly that word-level stress patterns 'would take further investigation'; his general impression is that in affixed words stress stays on the primary root and formatives (suffixes) are unstressed. Separately (p.92): the diphthongs /ai/ and /au/, which occur in open syllables in final or non-final position, 'are generally stressed'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. No acoustic or instrumental evidence; impressionistic, from eight years' residence (1953-62, Singhbhum District), work with Hoffmann's informant Menas Orea, tapes, and Langendoen's unpublished Mundari phonology.
new_statements.exceptions: Domain restriction: the closed-final/penult rule is asserted for morphemes only; words are root-stressed with unstressed formatives 'in general', pending investigation. Diphthongs /ai/, /au/ in open syllables are 'generally stressed' regardless of position (e.g. paisa 'money', cauli 'rice', bancau 'to save'), which can override the penult default. No lexical exceptions listed.
new_statements.identity_note: Cook describes Mundari as having two principal dialects, Hasada (SE Ranchi district around Sarwada; no phonemic aspiration, resists Hindi/Sadari loans) and Naguri (west of the Ranchi-Chaibasa road; phonemic aspiration, Hindi/Sadari loans), and treats Ho as effectively a Mundari dialect. His own exposure was among Mundas and Hos in Singhbhum District (1953-62) and his chief informant was Menas Orea of Buruma, Hoffmann's Encyclopedia Mundarica informant; the phoneme inventory he gives (no aspirates) matches Hasada. He does not say the stress rule is dialect-specific.

readall_conflicts: The one work opened here, Cook 1965, states a weight-conditioned rule counted from the right edge of the MORPHEME (final syllable stressed if closed, else penult; diphthongs generally stressed; in words stress stays on the root, suffixes unstressed) and explicitly leaves word-level stress uninvestigated. This stands against Hoffmann 1903's 'generally initial' accent (the other pole of the catalog's conflict record) for all closed-final disyllabic roots, and against Donegan 1993's family-level left-edge account on heavy-heavy (CVC.CVC) disyllables (Cook final, Donegan initial), while agreeing with Donegan on LL, HL, LH disyllables and LLL trisyllables and with the carried Osada 2008/Sinha 1975 report that trisyllables are not initial-stressed. The held Horo et al. 2023/2025 instrumental studies (per the existing statement) find no robust word-level prominence cue at all. No single placement is supported across sources, so the catalog's 'conflict' coding stands; Cook's own hedge that word stress 'would take further investigation' is itself evidence that the 1965 rule should not be read as a settled word-stress rule.

audit.recode_to: Keep 'conflict' unless the catalog schema has a kind for 'no demonstrable word-level stress / prominence phrasal-or-segmental only (instrumental)'; if it does, Mundari is a candidate once Horo, Anderson & Gogoi 2025 is read into the record (authors themselves call 4-speaker results premature, so a hedge is warranted).
